title: Dielectrics, Piezoelectrics and Ferroelectrics
description: Eight qualitative questions covering polarization, frequency response, dielectric loss, breakdown, piezoelectricity and ferroelectricity from the complete Dielectric w Piezo lecture. Multiple-response items use +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero.

questions.prompt: What happens when an ideal dielectric is polarized by an applied electric field?

options.content: Positive and negative bound charges shift slightly relative to one another.
A net dipole moment per unit volume can develop.
Bound polarization charge can appear at surfaces.
A steady flow of free carriers through the bulk is required for polarization.

questions.explanation: Polarization is the displacement or alignment of bound charge, producing electric dipoles and possibly bound surface charge. It does not require the continuous free-carrier transport that defines conduction current.

questions.prompt: Match the qualitative polarization mechanisms to physical motion. Which statements are correct?

options.content: Electronic polarization displaces an electron cloud relative to its nucleus.
Ionic polarization shifts positive and negative ion sublattices relative to each other.
Orientational polarization aligns permanent molecular dipoles.
Electronic polarization occurs only in molecules that already have permanent dipoles.

questions.explanation: Electronic polarization can occur in every atom because the electron cloud can distort. Ionic polarization involves relative ion displacement, while orientational polarization requires permanent dipoles that rotate toward the field.
questions.source: EE3431C Dielectric w Piezo, polarization mechanisms section

questions.prompt: As the frequency of an alternating electric field increases, which qualitative trends are expected in a dielectric?

options.content: Slower polarization mechanisms stop following the field first.
The real permittivity can decrease in stages as mechanisms drop out.
Dielectric loss can peak near a mechanism's relaxation frequency.
Every mechanism contributes more strongly without limit as frequency rises.

questions.explanation: A polarization mechanism contributes only while it can respond on the field's timescale. Slow mechanisms such as dipole rotation drop out before fast electronic polarization, causing dispersion and often a loss peak near relaxation.
questions.source: EE3431C Dielectric w Piezo, frequency response and relaxation section

questions.prompt: What is the most direct physical meaning of dielectric loss in an AC field?

options.content: Polarization lags the field, so some electrical energy is dissipated as heat.
All supplied energy is stored and returned with no phase lag.
The internal electric field is exactly zero at all times.
The electronic band gap has become infinite.

questions.explanation: Real polarization does not respond instantaneously. The lag between applied field and polarization produces an out-of-phase current component and converts part of the cycle's energy into heat.
questions.source: EE3431C Dielectric w Piezo, dielectric loss section

questions.prompt: Which statements about dielectric breakdown are correct?

options.content: Breakdown occurs when the electric field exceeds a material- and condition-dependent strength.
Local heating can increase conduction and create destructive positive feedback.
Defects, moisture and electrical aging can reduce practical breakdown strength.
Breakdown is always perfectly reversible once the voltage is removed.

questions.explanation: Breakdown strength depends on the material, geometry, temperature, defects and history. Thermal runaway and field-enhanced carrier processes can cause irreversible damage, so removal of voltage does not guarantee recovery.
questions.source: EE3431C Dielectric w Piezo, dielectric breakdown and aging section

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish the direct and converse piezoelectric effects?

options.content: The direct effect converts applied mechanical stress into electrical charge.
The converse effect converts an applied electric field into mechanical strain.
The two effects support sensor and actuator applications, respectively.
Every centrosymmetric crystal must be piezoelectric.

questions.explanation: Mechanical stress can produce charge in the direct effect, while an electric field can produce deformation in the converse effect. Piezoelectricity requires suitable non-centrosymmetric structure; centrosymmetry prevents a linear piezoelectric response.
questions.source: EE3431C Dielectric w Piezo, piezoelectricity section

questions.prompt: Which properties are characteristic of a ferroelectric material below its Curie temperature?

options.content: It can possess spontaneous polarization without an applied field.
An applied field can switch the polarization direction.
A polarization-electric-field hysteresis loop can occur.
A ferroelectric can never show piezoelectric behaviour.

questions.explanation: Ferroelectrics have switchable spontaneous polarization and therefore exhibit hysteresis. Their polar crystal phase is also piezoelectric; ferroelectricity is a more restrictive property, not one that excludes piezoelectricity.
questions.source: EE3431C Dielectric w Piezo, ferroelectricity and hysteresis section

questions.prompt: Inserting a linear dielectric between capacitor plates can increase capacitance because polarization reduces the effective internal field for a given amount of free plate charge.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: Bound polarization charges oppose part of the field from the free plate charges. Consequently, a larger free charge is required to reach the same voltage, which means the capacitance is increased by the dielectric permittivity.
questions.source: EE3431C Dielectric w Piezo, capacitive behaviour section
